📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you’re limited on space, don’t let the length of a rowing machine deter you. While there are many great rowing machines on the market, there are also some awesome compact alternatives that offer all the same tech features you’ll find in other cardio machines.

In a recent development, during our search for the best compact rowing machine, we found an array of excellent standalone options and options that fit in well with other top-rated home gym equipment. We considered the overall footprint and other key features, and scoured the reviews to see what owners had to say about each product. Below is our list of the best compact home rowing machines available.

According to recent reports, the rowing machines included in this list were carefully selected based on what most consumers would want out of a rowing machine, keeping in mind that they needed to have a smaller footprint and folding or upright storage options. We evaluated each choice based on size, portability, cost, high-tech features, versatility, and durability. We also scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each rowing machine.

According to recent reports, on the Hydrow website, the Hydrow Wave is rated 4.6/5 stars with over 9,000 reviews at the time of writing. It’s the brand’s compact, budget-friendly option for those who want to elevate their at-home workout routine. The length is just 80 inches, which is the shortest on this list, and the overall size is 30 percent shorter than the original Hydrow Rower. You cannot fold it, but there is the option to store it upright using The Hydrow Wave Vertical Anchor. This is a wall-mounted strap that holds the rower upright. It costs an additional $190, which is a bit on the pricey side.

It has been revealed that the frame is made of aluminum and steel. It has a flat anthracite polymer body, which is a durable and lightweight material. The handle has an ergonomic design for a low-stress grip, and the strap is made from water- and rot-resistant polyester webbing. It also has a patented electromagnetic drag system that mimics the experience of rowing on open water.

It has been revealed that overall, the reviews on the Hydrow website are positive, and many mention how quiet the machine is and how much they like the small footprint. One review notes, “The machine is such great quality. It’s quiet and sleek looking.” The critical reviews make up 3 percent of the overall reviews and state complications like non-working parts being delivered. However, Hydrow has responded to each review to resolve any issues.

Sources indicate that the NordicTrack RW700 has a 10-inch HD touchscreen you can tilt and pivot to follow along with an iFIT workout led by your favorite trainer on or off the rower. An iFIT subscription is $39 per month, and you’ll have access to live and on-demand classes. Membership to the fitness app is not required to use the rower; however, you won’t have access to trainer-led classes without it.

It has been revealed that A trainer-led rowing workout gives you the option to row on the open water for a more scenic experience, and there are also studio sessions. The resistance is adjusted automatically among 26 resistance levels during each class, so you don’t need to worry about stopping to make changes. The oversized foot pedals have adjustable nylon foot straps with quick release, which is excellent for those who want to incorporate movements off the rower into their workout.

The rail is 87 inches long and made from durable steel. It has an inertia-enhanced flywheel, so it should maintain a smooth rotation. If you have a shared space, the NordicTrack RW700 rower has a magnetic resistance system that creates tension against the flywheel without touching, making it a quieter option. After your workout, this magnetic rowing machine can be moved using the front wheels, but it can’t be folded.

In a recent development, the flywheel has been designed to maintain inertia and rotate smoothly, and the steel rail is oversized to help keep you stable. The large, pivoting foot pedals with adjustable nylon straps keep your feet in place, and the seat is molded with comfort in mind.

If you like to incorporate other movements into your rowing workout or train off of the rower, the Echelon Row-s has a 22-inch HD touchscreen that can be flipped 180 degrees. While an Echelon Fit subscription is not required, the extra $35/month workout app gives you access to over 40 live classes and more than 1,000 on-demand workouts from its library, including rowing, biking, running, and functional training classes.

It has been revealed that the ergonomic design of the seat and the ability to adjust the foot platforms to a comfortable position help you maintain proper posture and alignment. If you’re short on space, the length goes from 84 inches long to just 41 inches long when folded. On the Echelon website, this rower is rated 4.6/5 stars. “The machine looks great, operates very quietly, and gives a great workout no matter your level,” notes reviewer Brett P.

Dimensions: 87.02" L x 22.0" W x 47.24" H.

Storage: Folds in half for vertical storage.

Display: 10-inch smart HD touchscreen.

Available programming: Live and on-demand workouts, scenic rows.

Industry observers note that the NordicTrack RW600 balances great tech features and an accessible price, making it a great value. The 10-inch screen is an excellent option for those who want to take instructor-led classes using an iFIT membership. NordicTrack’s patented Silent Magnetic Resistance can be adjusted up to 26 levels automatically in an iFIT class or manually as needed.

Recent findings suggest that the pivoting foot pedals are oversized, and the nylon straps keep your feet secure. The handlebar has a soft grip, and the molded seat is designed to help you feel comfortable. When your workout is finished, the NordicTrack RW600 can be folded and stored out of the way.

What factors should you consider before you pull the trigger on a rower? Here’s what we’d recommend you take into account as you ponder your purchase decision:.

Once you’ve decided on your rower location, it’s a good idea to measure the length, width, and height of your space to determine what size machine works best. You’ll want to measure height to see if you have enough clearance for rowers to be stored upright.

According to recent reports, after measuring, think about how much you’re willing to spend. Take into consideration any additional costs such as a monthly subscription. Some rowers also have add-ons for purchase, such as a lumbar support system or seat upgrade.

In a recent development, ask yourself: How many levels of resistance do I need? Am I looking for an HD touchscreen with trainer-led classes or do I prefer a more simplistic display? Other features such as a magnetic resistance system may be crucial if you’re in a shared space and need a quieter machine. The rower’s maximum height and/or weight capacity may also play a role in your decision as well.

It has been revealed that rowing allows you to implement low-impact, cardio-based training, and you can adjust the resistance for a strength-focused session. It’s a full-body workout that uses 86 percent of your muscles. With each stroke, you’re using your core and legs for the initial pull and finishing the rowing movement by using your upper body. Since you’re in a seated position, there’s less pressure on your knee and ankle joints.

It has been revealed that getting all four types of exercise (endurance, strength, balance, and flexibility) has benefits, according to The National Institute of Health (NIH). A rowing machine can be utilized for two types: endurance and strength. Many rowing machines have built-in programs or subscriptions that offer classes geared toward building strength and endurance.

According to recent reports, rowing is a great way to build strength and endurance while working various muscle groups. There are choices to suit a variety of budgets with different storage options and sizes. Figuring out how much space you have, your price range and the features you’d like will help you choose the best compact rowing machine for you.

The machines on this list range from just over $700 to around $2,000. You can find a rower in your price range, but if you opt for a rower under, say, $200, you may be compromising quality.

Typically, rowing machine length ranges between six to nine feet with more compact options at six or seven feet long.

According to recent reports, the level of resistance that’s best for you depends on your fitness level, experience, and goals. Overall, you don’t want your workout to be too easy or so challenging you don’t accomplish the goal of your training session.

Compact rowing machines usually have air or magnetic resistance, and some options implement both.

Tech Report: Think Your Saddle Is Too High? The Signs Every Cyclist Should Know Before Their Next Ride

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours.
  • Industry observers note that and because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix.
  • To get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours. It can show up as pain behind the knee, pressure in the saddle, numbness, or that familiar feeling that you’re reaching for the pedal instead of driving through it.

Industry observers note that and because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix. Riders often blame the saddle itself, their bib shorts, or even their flexibility when the issue is simply that the seat is a little too high.

To get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change. Check out Bicycling’s Guide to the Perfect Bike Fit.

Recent findings suggest that that said, saddle height is also where fit advice gets messy. There isn’t one perfect number that works for everyone, and the usual rules of thumb are only starting points. Your ideal height depends on your body, your mobility, your injury history, your cleat setup, and more.

Quick Signs Your Saddle May Be Too High• Pain behind the knee • Saddle sores or numbness • Discomfort where your hamstrings meet your glutes • Rocking hips while pedaling • Reaching for the pedal at the bottom of the stroke Quick Fix• Lower the saddle a few millimeters, do a real ride, and reassess.

Here’s how to tell whether your saddle may be too high and a simple at-home check you can do before your next ride.

In a recent development, saddle height is one of the first things riders adjust, and for good reason. When it’s close, you feel smoother and more comfortable. When it’s off, the problems can spread everywhere.

But this is where people get tripped up: saddle height is key, but it is only one element in an interconnected system. If your cleats are in the wrong place, your saddle is too far forward or back, or your crankarms don’t suit you, changing saddle height alone may not solve much. It’s the beginning of fit, not the whole thing.

It has been revealed that A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel. Two riders with the same height and inseam may still end up at different saddle heights because bodies aren’t identical and neither are pedaling styles.

Pain is the clearest warning that something in your position needs attention. Riding is hard. Suffering through an interval is one thing. Pain caused by pressure, strain, or repeated irritation from a bad setup is another.

A saddle that’s too high often shows up in a few predictable ways:.

Recent findings suggest that this is the classic one. If you feel pain at the back of the knee, especially after longer rides or harder efforts, a too-high saddle is one possible cause.

According to recent reports, but not the only one. Fit problems tend to overlap. So treat this as a clue, not a verdict.

If the back of your pedal stroke feels strained, tight, or tuggy, especially when you’re trying to make power, your saddle may be a little high.+.

Recent findings suggest that A high saddle can make you unstable on the bike. Instead of sitting planted, you start shifting and searching. That extra motion can increase friction and pressure, which can mean hot spots, sores, and numbness.

If your hips are dropping side to side at the bottom of the pedal stroke, there’s a decent chance you’re compensating for too much saddle height.

Some riders point their toes naturally. But if you’re really reaching at the bottom of the stroke and compensating by going toes-down, that can be another sign the saddle is too high.

Sources indicate that rocking hips can also happen with a saddle that’s too low. So can a toes-down pedaling style. Tight hamstrings, limited mobility, weak core stability, and other fit complications can all muddy the picture. Back-of-knee pain can come from saddle height, but it can also come from saddle fore-aft, cleat setup, or a combination of things.

According to recent reports, that doesn’t make the signs worthless. It just means you should think in patterns, not absolutes.

If you have knee pain plus hip rocking plus pressure and instability in the saddle, now the case gets stronger.

Todd Carver, Specialized’s human performance manager, shared a simple check that can help flag a saddle that may be too high.

If the distance from heel to pedal is more than about one centimeter, your saddle could be too high.

The result is a prompt to look closer, not a green light to make significant changes without further investigation.

Sources indicate that don’t make a giant change. That’s how you turn one problem into several problems.

Start small. Lower the saddle a few millimeters at a time, then ride it long enough to notice whether the change actually helps. One short spin around the block is not enough. You want enough ride time to see whether the pain eases, whether your pedaling feels smoother, and whether you stop shifting around on the saddle.

If you’re dealing with persistent pain, don’t keep self-diagnosing forever.

A good fit pro can sort out whether saddle height is the actual problem or just the most obvious symptom.

In a recent development, riders fixate on saddle height because it feels fundamental. And it is. But it’s also just one part of a system.

A high saddle can absolutely cause trouble. So can cleat position. So can saddle setback. So can crank length. So can your mobility. The goal is not to chase some magic formula you found online. It’s to get to a position that lets you pedal smoothly, make power comfortably, and finish rides feeling worked, not damaged.

That’s why the best takeaway is a modest one: use the common signs, do a quick check, make small changes, and listen to what your body tells you.

Latest Update: Josh Kerr Claims You Probably Don’t Need Water for Runs Under 12 Miles. The Internet Had Thoughts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant.
  • Industry observers note that so when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from.
  • "I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr said, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I've worn a hydration vest exactly once, and it was less than pleasant. The two bottles bounced loosely against my chest, with water leaking down my shirt throughout the run. It was not a flattering look. Every step came with its own sloshing soundtrack. I spent so much time adjusting the thing (despite an across-the-chest strap) that I barely enjoyed my run.

Industry observers note that so when Josh Kerr recently suggested that recreational runners might be going a little overboard with their hydration gear, I understood where he was coming from. During a Reddit AMA hosted by BBC Sport, the Scottish middle-distance star, who casually broke the mile world record in July with a 3:42.66 finish, shared his thoughts on the growing popularity of running vests.

"I'd say that if you're running less than 12 miles, you probably don't need to bring water bottles with you," Kerr said, adding that people running in cities can generally stop at a store if they need something to drink.

For context, we're talking about a world-record holder, Olympic medalist, and world champion in the 1500 meters. He knows a thing or two about logging miles. And while 12 miles might look quite different on his watch than mine, I don't think his suggestion was particularly outrageous.

And because everything is contested on the internet, plenty of people disagree.

Runner @natalie.the.capn shared Kerr's comments on Threads and explained that she wears a hydration belt on every outing so she has somewhere to keep her phone, particularly in case of an emergency. "Funny how men rarely think of that," she wrote.

I do understand her concern. I'm a guy, so I'm definitely not going to pretend I have the same safety considerations that women often face while exercising alone. I also bring my phone everywhere, usually carrying it in my hand because iPhones only get bigger and the pockets on most of my running shorts haven't kept up.

She also pointed out that some of her routes take her six miles or more between places where she can get water, which is an entirely different experience from mine.

Recent findings suggest that I live in Latest York City, where Central Park has plenty of water fountains (that work ... most of the time) and there's usually a deli within walking distance to snag a Gatorade. I can see why Kerr's approach makes sense here, especially for shorter runs. I've also tried handheld bottles and waist straps, and neither has been particularly enjoyable. Between the bouncing, adjusting, and occasional hand cramps, I'd love to carry as little as possible in my hands.

In a recent development, that changes a lot during marathon training, something I've put myself through four times now, when I'm out for considerably longer and need water to wash down those pasty gels. Aside from the hydration aspect, stopping to buy something, pausing my watch, and interrupting my stride halfway through a long run is a vibe killer.

Industry observers note that and I'm certainly not arguing against being prepared. I learned the hard way that sunscreen deserved a permanent spot in my prerun routine after years of neglecting it ended with some casual skin cancer surgery.

It has been revealed that the Threads debate, naturally, has brought out some pretty different opinions. One commenter, siding with Kerr, wrote, "Yeah im gonna listen to the guy who runs for a living but thanks." Others pointed out that beginners, slower runners, and people training in hot weather could have very different hydration needs.

They're definitely right about that. Twelve miles is a long way for plenty of runners, no matter what their experience level, and access to water, weather, pace, and individual needs all change the equation. Kerr even acknowledged that people have different reasons for carrying gear, something that seems to have gotten a little lost as his comments made their way around social media.

It has been revealed that I still think he has a fair point about how much equipment we sometimes convince ourselves we need on a run. That stated, if your vest makes your runs more comfortable or gives you peace of mind, by all means wear it. For me, I'll be keeping my phone close and bringing an appropriate amount of water when I need it.

As for my hydration vest, it's been collecting dust ever since that first outing, and I haven't missed it one bit.

Recent findings suggest that sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

According to recent reports, there are plenty of reasons to start riding inside. Questionable weather, overly packed schedules, and less daylight can cause outdoor riders to head inside for some indoor saddle time. It’s also possible you’re someone who doesn’t ride outside and you just want a good low-impact workout in the comfort of your own home—without breaking the bank.

According to recent reports, recently we did extensive testing in the office on different exercise bikes. I found that some people who don’t ride bikes outside may actually prefer some of the less expensive exercise bike options. Some of the higher-end exercise bikes we tested feel like a real bike outside—and pair with specific apps like Zwift for when you want to get some group rides or racing in. If you aren’t used to a bike outside, then getting comfortable in that position can be a hard transition. More narrow saddles, a more aggressive position, and controls that simulate the shifters on a bike may not be what you want. Largely, these more inexpensive exercise bikes have more upright positions, wider and more padded saddles, and controls that would resemble the exercise bike you might see on the floor of a fitness center.

Keep in mind that inexpensive is relative—the bikes we have on this list range from about $200 up to $700. If you’re looking to boost your mood, stay consistent, or supplement your training with an affordable indoor cycling bike, these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best mix of value, performance, and reliability.

If you're further along in your indoor training journey and none of the bikes on this list feel like the right fit, take a look at our reviews of the Peloton, Zwift Ride V2, and other premium models.

Industry observers note that this budget-priced, belt-driven bike operates a 35-pound flywheel that provides a smooth and quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable via a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately, if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches, and allows riders to adjust the handlebar height as well as the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Using the single-button monitor, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned as you exercise. Just below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame is designed to provide stability and durability, but it's easy to move if you tip it up onto the small wheels on the front edge.

Besides being designed to look like an entry-level Peloton, the Yesoul S3’s biggest selling point is its Bluetooth connectivity, which pairs with the Yesoul Sports App (on both iOS and Android) and works with Zwift and other interactive training apps. All your workout data, including distance, time, calories burned, speed, heart rate, odometer, and cadence, is tracked and easy to access.

It has been revealed that the bike has a quiet belt drive and magnetic resistance, with 100 levels that are easy to adjust with a knob. With a height- and distance-adjustable seat and handlebar, the S3 is built to fit riders from 4-feet-9-inches to 6-feet-2-inches—though riders at the higher end of that range and those with disproportionately longer legs might find the riding position to feel a bit “off.” The bike is easy to move on two small transport wheels, and it comes in both white and black models for a sleek, Peloton-like aesthetic.

Sources indicate that this is a fantastic price for a budget bike that delivers a Peloton-like experience. It has the same sleek silhouette, with a saddle that adjusts both up/down and fore/aft, plus an adjustable handlebar height—just like the real thing. The belt-drive system is another major plus, keeping noise to a minimum so the only sounds you hear are your own effort (and hopefully some music to cover it up).

Industry observers note that to keep costs down, this bike skips the large built-in display, instead offering a tablet holder and Bluetooth connectivity. That means you can ride with any third-party app you prefer—including Peloton classes—using your own device. At this price, it’s a fair trade-off. But if you want a built-in screen, Merach offers a similar model with that feature for about $450 more.

It has been revealed that merach’s newest bike, the A26 Aura, is one of the best Peloton competitors I’ve seen. The seat adjusts up and down as well as fore and aft, and the handlebar also moves vertically for a comfortable fit.

At its current sale price, the Merach A26 Aura makes a compelling case as one of the best values on this list.

Sources indicate that the Echelon Connect Sport 2 delivers a Peloton-like experience at a more affordable price. However, some shorter riders have reported difficulty positioning the saddle close enough to the handlebars for a comfortable fit.

The bike has the standard DualTrack console shared by similar-level Schwinn and Nautilus products, which has two sharp, backlit LCD screens loaded with 29 workouts.

The seat and handlebar adjust by height and angle to fit owners from 4-feet-6-inches to 6-feet-6-inches; however, as always, those at the far ends of the range might have more difficulty getting a comfortable fit. Ultimately, the bike is a solid package for the price—especially if you can catch one on sale for around $400.

According to recent reports, looking for a cheap home exercise bike that will neither take over your space nor break the bank? When not in use, this compact device folds down to half its size and can be easily rolled into a closet or tucked under a bed.

According to recent reports, while it may have a minimalist design, it still has the basic functionality needed for a workout. It touts 12 levels of magnetic resistance, adjusted via a knob below the handlebar, that allows you to adjust the intensity as needed. The built-in LCD screen, although very basic, keeps track of key workout stats, including distance, time, speed, calories burned, and heart rate.

Users love how quiet this bike is, making it perfect for multitasking or watching TV while riding. Though it may not provide the high resistance some hardcore riders seek, many praise it as a “sturdy, well-built machine” with a “comfortable seat and great height adjustability.”.

Just like with a regular bicycle, if you want the best experience on your indoor bike, it’s key to get the proper fit. Josh Taylor, a global brand ambassador for the online fitness site Spinning, recommends finding an indoor cycling bike that puts you in the same position as the bike you’re accustomed to riding outside.

For example, if your daily rider is a road bike, look for an indoor cycling bike with a handlebar option that incorporates a traditional bullhorn bar and mimics the hand-position options of drops and brake hoods. However, if you’re already used to taking studio classes, an indoor cycling bike with just the traditional bullhorn-style bar will work great, says Ben Sharp, three-time Order of Ikkos medal recipient and founder of Sharp Coaching.

In a recent development, if you don’t ride at all outside or in a spin class yet, then it will take a bit more playing around with the exercise bike to figure out sizing and position. Start with getting saddle height set up correctly, then if you can adjust reach to the handlebars that’s step two. For the reach shoot to have a slight bend in the elbows and remember to keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. Matt Phillips, Senior Test Editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on dialing in saddle height. What applies to saddle height on an outdoor bike largely applies to exercise bikes as well. “A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel,” says Phillips.

Join Bicycling All Access for more in-depth gear reviews.

According to recent reports, when you’re riding an outdoor bike, you’re mostly working against inertia as you pedal. In order to recreate that sensation and effort on a stationary bike, manufacturers have to simulate that resistance in some way. Most choose to use a fan or a flywheel (a weighted disc that spins as you pedal).

Recent findings suggest that flywheels work by storing inertia as they spin, and smoothing out the pedal stroke to eliminate that choppy up and down motion you’d otherwise experience. For most budget spin bikes, a heavier flywheel means a smoother ride, though some bikes opt for a light (8-pound) flywheel that maintains its inertia by spinning four times as fast instead.

In a recent development, since the pedals on spin bikes are fixed to the flywheel (no coasting), the smooth-moving mechanism helps keep your pedaling consistent. These bikes will usually have a knob or lever that allows you to adjust the resistance, making it harder or easier to pedal, independent of your cadence (how fast you’re spinning the pedals). If you’re used to riding a bike outside, then think about it like riding a fixed-gear bike or fixie.

Fan-operated resistance bikes are a bit simpler: As you pedal, the fan blades push against the air around the machine. Your cadence is directly related to the amount of effort required to push the pedals, meaning these bikes don’t allow you to spin at a fast cadence with low resistance, which can be nice for warming up or cooling down.

Check out some highlights from the collection below, and shop the full lineup at Ciele.com.

Industry observers note that the beauty of this hat is its simplicity: a straightforward cap that lets merino wool's natural performance shine. Made from pure merino, it fits snugly, so it won’t shift while running, and the knit fabric naturally traps heat, vents excess moisture, and resists odors. Added bonus: This hat is machine washable (on the cold setting), and the “speedway” pattern gives it a snazzy look, too.

Recent findings suggest that prefer a more classic “watch cap” style beanie? Check out the VNTBeanie, also made from 100 percent merino fabric. You’ll get all the performance benefits of merino, plus the hat’s ribbed structure boosts its breathability (and looks great, too).

The snug fit and thumbholes make it easy to layer under a jacket and gloves, but it’s also great in warmer weather—the fabric is rated UPF 30, so it protects you from sunburn when worn on its own.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when someone states they want to lose weight, what they really mean is they want to shed excess body fat.
  • According to recent reports, protein plays a multifaceted role in weight management, influencing factors like hunger levels, metabolism, and muscle preservation.
  • The best protein powders provide a convenient and lean source of the muscle-building macronutrient, helping you hit your daily protein goals while also maintaining a calorie deficit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when someone states they want to lose weight, what they really mean is they want to shed excess body fat. However, without a well-designed strategy in place, a calorie deficit leads you to lose both fat and valuable muscle tissue. To minimize muscle loss, it’s crucial to incorporate resistance training, quality sleep, and a high-protein diet into your regular routine.

According to recent reports, protein plays a multifaceted role in weight management, influencing factors like hunger levels, metabolism, and muscle preservation. While heavy resistance training provides the necessary stimulus, signaling to the body that existing muscle should be retained, a high-protein diet ensures the body has an ample supply of amino acids. This prevents your body from metabolizing muscle tissue for energy.

The best protein powders provide a convenient and lean source of the muscle-building macronutrient, helping you hit your daily protein goals while also maintaining a calorie deficit. We tested more than 100 protein powders and selected nine products we think are best for weight loss.

Sources indicate that this content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

We chose these products based on a number of factors, including:.

Sources indicate that I chose Transparent Labs as the best protein powder for weight loss because it has a very high ratio of protein to the total number of calories: 28 grams to 130 calories. This helps you maximize protein consumption during a caloric deficit, which helps prevent you from losing muscle while you’re losing weight. It’s also third-party tested, Informed Choice certified, and completely artificial ingredient-free. And it comes in 15 flavor options.

I’ve tried a number of different flavors from Transparent Labs and Chocolate Peanut Butter is by far my favorite, followed closely by Mocha. I found they mixed easily in both a blender and a conventional shaker bottle. Whenever I’m trying to cut weight, I find this delicious protein powder helps curb my sweet tooth and tide me over between meals.

While I didn’t personally experience this, some customer reviews mention it can be challenging to get in contact with Transparent Labs’ customer service team.

Jacked Factory Authentic Iso has 25 grams of protein per serving, 2 grams of carbohydrates, and just 0.5 grams of fat, which is the least amount of fat of any powder on our list. If you’re looking to lose weight, this macronutrient profile will help keep you on the right track. However, something to keep in mind: This protein powder is sweetened with sucralose, which is an artificial sweetener—studies link these sweeteners to increased cancer risk. Additionally, unlike most brands on our list, Jacked Factory doesn’t do third-party testing on its products. This means there isn’t a guarantee the ingredients are pure and match the ingredient label.

Sources indicate that kessler tried Jacked Factory Authentic Iso and was impressed. “This is the only protein powder I’ve tried that didn’t settle at all,” he says. “I found it a bit too sweet, but if you’re looking for a powder that tastes like dessert, you should opt for this one.”.

If you’re looking for one of the best vegan protein powders that also works with a weight loss diet, Ka’Chava is a great choice. This vegan protein powder is marketed as a “whole-body meal,” which means it’s designed as a meal replacement rather than an addition to a meal or snack, like the other protein powders on our list. That’s why the calorie, carbohydrate, and fat counts (240, 25 grams, and 7 grams, respectively), are higher. The carb count is high for those on a low-carb diet, so that’s something to look out for. However, it packs in 25 grams of plant protein, derived from a combination of peas, brown rice, and quinoa, which will help preserve muscle while on a weight loss diet.

Tester Zoe Ettinger, a C.N.C.-in-training, uses this protein powder often. “I’m a big fan of Ka’Chava. It tastes delicious mixed in a smoothie with some frozen blueberries,” she notes. “I also like that it also has adaptogens, probiotics, greens, and probiotics. I notice a difference in how good I feel when I take Ka’Chava regularly,” she says.

Sources indicate that one thing to note about Ka’Chava is that it is the most expensive option on our list at $79.99 for a 15-serving bag. While the price reflects the fact that this protein powder is intended as a meal replacement, it’s still a significant investment.

According to recent reports, I chose Nutricost as the best protein powder for weight loss available on Amazon because its calorie and macronutrient profile is ideal for shedding pounds. Nutricost has a high protein content per serving, which is important for weight loss as protein can help enhance satiety and preserve muscle mass while in a deficit. With minimal fat and carbohydrates, this protein ensures you get the maximum protein intake without the added calories, making it an ideal choice for those looking to lose weight efficiently.

Sources indicate that the taste and mixability of this protein are also top-notch. I tested the Vanilla flavor; it blended excellently in both milk and water and had an authentic vanilla taste profile. Despite using artificial sweeteners, which often make products sickly sweet, I found the sweetness level to be on point. However, if you’re trying to avoid artificial sweeteners, choose Promix or Transparent Labs, which use natural sweeteners.

Sources indicate that huel is our favorite meal replacement for weight loss because it has a great protein-to-carb ratio. Huel has 40 grams of protein per serving, the most of any protein powder on our list, and 24 grams of carbs. While this might be more carbs than ideal for those on a keto diet, it’s a solid portion for most. Carbs are an essential nutrient and according to experts, you can consume 100 to 150 grams a day and still lose weight.

Industry observers note that kessler tried Huel in Chocolate and Vanilla. “The Chocolate flavor was great, probably because it uses real cocoa powder, which gave it an authentic chocolate flavor,” he says. “The Vanilla wasn’t as good—it didn’t really taste like vanilla and had an artificial aftertaste.” He notes that it doesn’t mix very well, but says it made him feel great. “Other similar products, like Transparent Labs Mass Gainer, give me an upset stomach. But I felt great after taking Huel Black Edition,” he says.

It has been revealed that promix is our favorite clean protein powder because it’s third-party tested and results are easily viewable on Promix’s website. Those results show this product is tested for heavy metals and verified gluten-free. And beyond these positive results, this protein powder has one of the most simple formulas on our list. Vanilla, for example, has just four ingredients, and Promix doesn’t use any artificial ingredients.

In a recent development, this protein powder, like others on our list, has a solid protein-to-carb ratio for weight loss (25 grams to 7 grams, respectively). A 2020 study found consuming a higher portion of protein versus carbs helped participants lose weight and prevented them from gaining the weight back.

In a recent development, I tried the Vanilla flavor of this protein powder. I enjoyed it for the most part, but it wasn’t quite sweet enough for my taste. And I wish it mixed a little better—there were some clumps after mixing.

One thing to note about Promix is that while it has been third-party tested, it hasn’t been third-party tested for sport specifically. This means it hasn’t been tested for substances banned in athletic competitions. So if you’re an athlete planning to compete, opt for a powder that’s Informed Sport Certified or NSF Certified for Sport.

In a recent development, one of my favorite casein protein powders is Casein+ from Legion Athletics. I chose Casein+ because it’s all-natural, meaning it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors, and it’s third-party tested by Labdoor for purity and potency. This product provides 25 grams of protein per serving and only contains 110 calories, regardless of the flavor you choose. This protein-to-calorie ratio is ideal for weight loss.

Along with whey, casein is a type of protein found in milk and is characterized by its slow digestion and absorption. This prolonged digestion makes it an ideal option for people looking to manage hunger levels and maintain a consistent supply of amino acids over an extended timeframe—such as during sleep or when going a long time between meals. By providing a steady stream of protein to the muscles, casein helps mitigate the risk of muscle breakdown that often accompanies calorie restriction. As a result, incorporating a casein protein powder into your diet can be a strategic move to help support your weight loss goals.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., tried the Dutch Chocolate flavor, saying it reminded him of a dark chocolate bar that isn’t too rich or too sweet. The only downside is that casein protein has a different consistency than whey. It’s generally thicker and often takes longer to dissolve. Lunsford noticed this during his testing, saying the product had a “slightly chalky aftertaste.”.

Naked Whey’s Unflavored protein stands out for its simplicity and purity; its single-ingredient formula consists of whey protein concentrate sourced for grass-fed cows. This simplicity aligns with the brand’s commitment to transparency, priding itself on avoiding additives, fillers, or artificial ingredients in its products.

With its neutral taste profile, this protein powder is very versatile, letting you integrate the protein powder seamlessly into your favorite recipes or smoothies without altering the flavor profile. Kessler tried the Unflavored version and states it “has a very slight vanilla taste to it.” He also detected a note of earthiness, but says “It would be really good mixed into a smoothie.” However, he mentions the two-scoop serving size can feel like a lot, so he recommends using extra liquid when blending it.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re someone who prefers a flavored protein powder, you’ll be happy to know Naked also offers five flavored options, including Chocolate, Vanilla, Strawberry, Chocolate Peanut Butter, and Double Chocolate. Naked only uses coconut sugar to sweeten its protein supplements, which isn’t nearly as sweet as artificial sweeteners like sucralose or acesulfame potassium.

We chose Sports Research as our best protein powder for weight loss and muscle gain because it has a solid protein-to-calorie ratio (25 grams to 140 calories), is Informed Sport Certified, is fairly priced at $1.20 per serving, and tastes great, according to testers.

Industry observers note that from a nutritional standpoint, Sports Research stacks up well against many of its competitors. The per-serving content for protein (25 grams), calories (140), and carbs (2 grams) compares favorably with most of the choices on our list, although the fat per serving (3.5 grams for Vanilla and 4 grams for Dutch Chocolate) is on the high side. Other ingredients include vitamin D, which has been linked to muscle health in recent research.

According to recent reports, tester Cory Kessler, C.N.C., C.P.T., tried the Creamy Vanilla flavor. “When I mixed it with milk it almost tasted like vanilla ice cream,” he notes. “But when I mixed it with water it diluted the flavor, and all I could taste was the sweetness,” he warns. He also notes that it mixed very well, and “wasn’t gritty or clumpy at all.”.

Whether from powder or whole food sources, protein aids weight loss mainly by:.

According to recent reports, protein powder can be an effective tool in helping you achieve your weight loss goals. Drinking a protein powder shake or smoothie provides a quick, easy way to consume high amounts of protein with a limited amount of calories, fat, and carbohydrates. One of the main benefits of protein powder is that it’s often extremely lean, with a very high ratio of protein to total number of calories. This makes protein powder an efficient way to hit your daily protein target while adhering to your calorie guidelines.

According to recent reports, choose a protein powder with a significant amount of protein, typically around 25 grams per serving. If you have weight loss goals, a whey, soy, or pea protein isolate is likely your best bet since they are ultra-filtered to remove excess carbohydrates and fats.

Sources indicate that when you have weight loss goals, it’s best to choose a protein powder with a moderate calorie count per serving, e.g., 100 to 160 calories. You should also ensure the majority of those calories come from protein, as this will best support your weight loss progress. Remember, protein is four calories per gram, so you can expect a supplement that has 25 grams of protein to have around 110 to 120 calories if it’s extremely lean.

It’s important to check the ingredients list of the supplement to ensure the product is free from added sugars or unnecessary fillers. Although these ingredients may contribute to the flavor, sweetness, and creaminess of the supplement, they often come with added calories. It’s generally best to select protein powders with minimal ingredients.

Sources indicate that occasionally, protein powders contain ingredients such as creatine, probiotics, or branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). While these aren’t necessary, it’s important to assess whether these added ingredients align with your health and fitness goals, and whether it’s worth choosing a protein powder that offers these options.

According to recent reports, regardless of your goals, choose a protein powder with a flavor and consistency you enjoy. I know this seems obvious, but if you dislike the taste, then you’re far less likely to use the protein powder on a consistent basis, if at all.

As a certified nutrition coach, I advise my clients to choose a protein powder that’s been third-party tested for quality, purity, and safety, especially when I’m working with athletes. This ensures your supplement is free from contaminants, including banned substances, and is deemed safe for consumption. Third-party testing also holds supplement companies accountable, providing assurance that the ingredients in the product align with the information provided on the supplement facts label.

Whenever you’re purchasing a dietary supplement, you should look for one that aligns with your specific health and fitness goals. With weight loss in mind, it’s typically recommended to avoid products with added sugars, or excessive amounts of carbohydrates and fats. Some consumers may also choose to avoid products with artificial additives, such as sweeteners, flavors, and colors, which are routinely found in protein powder supplements. If you’re looking for an all-natural protein powder with minimal ingredients, consider Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey or protein powders from Naked Nutrition.

As a certified nutrition coach, I think it’s important to emphasize that a protein powder isn’t a necessity for weight loss success. However, due to its convenience and effectiveness, it does offer some notable benefits when used as part of a holistic approach to weight loss that includes resistance training, quality sleep, and healthy lifestyle habits. Consuming a high-protein diet, especially during a weight-loss phase, helps manage hunger levels and improves muscle preservation. If a protein powder can help you hit your daily protein targets while still maintaining a calorie deficit, then I think it’s worth incorporating into your regular routine.

Protein shakes are an excellent way to help preserve lean muscle mass when pursuing your weight loss goals. If weight loss is your primary objective, I’d suggest opting for a whey protein isolate, such as Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey. This protein powder is incredibly lean, meaning the majority of calories come from protein alone. This can help you achieve your daily protein targets without over-consuming calories from the additional carbohydrates and fats commonly found in a whey protein concentrate.

Industry observers note that weight loss strategies vary from person to person, however, individuals with weight loss goals should aim for at least 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight. (This equates to approximately 0.5 to 0.7 grams of protein per pound of body weight.) This range should provide enough protein to support muscle mass while maintaining a calorie deficit, which is necessary for weight loss.

With protein powder for weight loss, certain protein sources are considered “leaner” than others. For example, whey protein isolates benefit from various kinds of processing and filtration that lower the fat and carbohydrates in the finished product. The main drawback with some plant-based proteins is that they can be naturally higher in carbs. Fortunately, high-quality plant protein powders could deliver comparable results to whey protein in terms of promoting lean body mass.Lean animal proteins include chicken breast, fish, and eggs. Even certain cuts of beef (sirloin) and pork (loin) are considered lean. Greek yogurt, tofu, beans, and lentils are among the non-animal sources of lean protein.

It has been revealed that when focusing on weight loss, it’s best to steer clear of calorie-rich beverages such as sugary sodas and sports drinks, fruit juices, and alcohol. Instead, choose options like water, seltzer, black coffee, and unsweetened tea, all of which are essentially calorie-free. Avoiding calorie-dense beverages allows you to allocate those calories to food instead, which should help improve your satiety or feelings of fullness after meals.

There’s no protein that targets belly fat loss specifically. However, prioritizing lean protein, such as a whey protein isolate, can be beneficial for your overall weight loss goals. Whey protein isolates are processed to minimize the carbohydrate and fat content, maximizing the protein-to-calorie ratio of the supplement. This makes them an efficient option to support your intake of dietary protein while maintaining a calorie deficit.

This Coach’s Fartlek Workout Is One of the Best for Learning a Crucial Running Skill

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success.
  • Learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World.
  • In a recent development, moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re racing your dream marathon or tackling a weekly speed workout, finding the right pace is crucial to your success. Go out too hard and you may struggle to hold on. Run too conservatively and you might miss your goal finish.

Learning to recognize different paces takes practice, run coach Matt Fitzgerald, cofounder of 80/20 endurance, tells Runner’s World. One workout he recommends for building this skill is a fartlek he learned from fellow run coach Brad Hudson, his coauthor on the book, Run Faster from the 5K to the Marathon: How to Be Your Own Best Coach.

In a recent development, moving you through several race paces, this workout challenges you to find the subtle differences between them. The goal? Building both aerobic fitness and a greater sense of pace control.

This workout helps improve your ability to settle into the right effort earlier, as well as enhance your capacity to hold those paces for longer—a perfect session for both optimizing your weekly speed run and helping you run your fastest race.

After an easy running warmup, you’ll run five faster segments, separated by an easy jog of the same duration.

Industry observers note that the base workout uses three target paces: 5K pace for the one-minute segments, 10K pace for the two-minute segments, and half-marathon pace for the three-minute segment. If you don’t know your race paces, you can also go off of rate of perceived exertion (RPE), with 10 equaling all-out effort. You should still be able to have a conversation around 4 RPE.

Sources indicate that fitzgerald states the workout should feel “fun hard,” meaning the faster running should feel challenging, but you shouldn’t finish the workout feeling like you just went all out in a race. Each surge is relatively short, so focus on hitting your intended effort rather than pushing as hard as you can.

According to recent reports, more experienced, higher-volume runners can extend the pyramid to 1-2-3-2-1-2-3-2-1, again jogging for the same duration after each faster segment. This version includes 17 minutes of faster running and 17 minutes of recovery jogging, compared to just nine minutes of each in the original version.

In Fitzgerald’s experience, many runners tend to think of their effort in two broad categories: slow and fast, but this workout challenges that by demanding more care in differentiating between faster paces.

Sources indicate that the one-minute 5K pace efforts should be faster than the two-minute 10K pace efforts, which should be faster than the three-minute half-marathon effort, explains Fitzgerald. The differences between these three paces are small—often just a few seconds per mile—so learning to recognize what each one feels like can help you become a more efficient and more confident runner.

Before each segment, think about the effort you’re trying to find. For the first one-minute interval, Fitzgerald suggests literally imagining that you’re starting a 5K race. You wouldn’t want to sprint the opening minute of that race and flame out, so resist that urge here, too.

It has been revealed that try to settle into the right pace by feel, then use your watch to check and adjust. Over time, you’ll grow more attuned to the connection between how you feel and how fast you’re moving. “Your watch can’t [run the workout] for you,” Fitzgerald states. “It can tell you how fast you’re going. It can’t tell you how fast you should go.”.

Sources indicate that learning to run by feel translates to race day, when you want to hit your goal pace. Your body’s response to the conditions and the effort helps you decide how to proceed through each mile, slowing down or speeding up.

Sources indicate that this workout doesn’t ask you to spend a long time at any single pace. Instead, it gives you short exposures to several intensities within one session.

Hudson, who’s coached multiple Olympians and world-class athletes, tells Runner’s World that moving through a range of paces during a single workout helps with not only pace control, but also running economy or the energy required to run at a given speed.

Additionally, Hudson explains the continuous nature of the fartlek session gives it an aerobic emphasis because you never actually stop running throughout the entirety of the workout. “The faster portions [of the workout] increase oxygen demand, but as you go longer in a workout, the more it becomes aerobic, no matter what,” he states. “If you’re keeping the running continuous, the aerobic energy systems just keep going up and up and up.”.

According to recent reports, fitzgerald agrees, although he also notes athletes get some anaerobic stress during the shorter, faster efforts. Think of it as a way to work on several aspects of your fitness at once, rather than a session designed to train just one. Plus, switching between paces can make the workout more mentally engaging than returning to the same effort over and over again.

In a recent development, the first time you try the workout, you might overshoot a target pace or find it difficult to feel the difference between efforts. That’s okay. Fitzgerald says trial and error is an key part of developing the skill.

Sources indicate that when you repeat the session, look for signs that your pacing is becoming more controlled: You start each segment closer to your intended effort, settle into a steadier rhythm, and maintain a clear difference between your 5K, 10K, and half marathon paces. You may also find it easier to keep your recovery jogs consistent.

Industry observers note that the point is, you don’t need to nail every second of this workout. Learn from your mistakes, adjust when necessary, and remember Fitzgerald’s advice: “Progress over perfection.”.

Recent findings suggest that it may be tempting to think of the easy jogs simply as passing time between hard segments. But both coaches emphasize the value of continuous running and implore runners not to lose focus during the recovery intervals.

Sources indicate that fitzgerald says teaching your body to recover from a faster effort while still moving presents a unique challenge. Your muscles must learn how to continue producing the energy needed to keep you running efficiently while your body works to recover from the harder interval at the same time. This adaptation translates directly to race day when you have to settle back into race pace after surging to pass another runner or gliding a little too fast down a hill.

Industry observers note that the key is paying attention to how your recovery intervals feel. If you have to slow them down more and more to prepare for the next segment, Fitzgerald indicates that may be a sign you’re pushing the faster portions too hard.

The beauty of this workout is if you realize you’ve gone out too quickly, you can easily adjust so you can still complete the workout. If you overcooked one of your speedier segments, Fitzgerald suggests tacking on another minute or so to the easy jog until you breathe easier and lower your heart rate—then adjust your effort level on the next interval.

Because the workout touches several intensity levels, Fitzgerald recommends it during base training or in the off-season. It can help runners maintain well-rounded fitness before they begin building toward a more specific goal.

It has been revealed that it can also work as the de facto speed workout during a lighter training week or serve as a secondary quality workout during half-marathon or marathon training. In this case, the session offers a chance to maintain some faster running while the biggest emphasis remains on your long runs and race-specific efforts.

Industry observers note that hudson uses the workout as a key tool in returning to training post-marathon. After a week off, he generally has his athletes begin with easy running. Then, he adds this workout as a way to reintroduce different intensity levels and prepare his athletes for more demanding work ahead.

Whenever you use it, keep its purpose in mind: It’s designed to help you practice changing gears and build general fitness, and using it to support key workouts specifically tailored to your next race makes it even more effective.
